texts.label: text
texts.orig: METHODS In this monocentric, prospective, single-blind randomized controlled trial, 739 patients undergoing coronary procedures were included and randomized to a fasting or a nonfasting strategy. Emergency procedures were excluded. The primary endpoint was a composite of vasovagal reaction, hypoglycemia (de fi ned by blood sugar # 0.7 g/L), and isolated nausea and/or vomiting. Noninferiority margin was 4%. Secondary endpoints were contrast-induced nephropathy and patients ' satisfaction.
texts.text: METHODS In this monocentric, prospective, single-blind randomized controlled trial, 739 patients undergoing coronary procedures were included and randomized to a fasting or a nonfasting strategy. Emergency procedures were excluded. The primary endpoint was a composite of vasovagal reaction, hypoglycemia (de fi ned by blood sugar # 0.7 g/L), and isolated nausea and/or vomiting. Noninferiority margin was 4%. Secondary endpoints were contrast-induced nephropathy and patients ' satisfaction.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: RESULTS Among the 739 procedures (697 elective and 42 semiurgent), 517 angiographies, and 222 angioplasties (including complex and high-risk procedures) were performed. The primary endpoint occurred in 30 of 365 nonfasting patients (8.2%) vs 37 of 374 fasting patients (9.9%), demonstrating noninferiority (absolute between-group difference, − 1.7%; 1-sided 95% CI upper limit: 1.8%). No food-related adverse event occurred, and contrast-related acute kidney injuries were similar between groups. Overall, procedure satisfaction and perceived pain were similar in both groups, but nonfasting patients reported less hunger and thirst ( P < 0.01). In case of redo coronary procedures, most patients (79%) would choose a nonfasting strategy.

texts.orig: In the fi eld of interventional neuroradiology procedures, also performed under local anesthesia, no differences in safety were found between fasting and nonfasting patients in a large prospective nonrandomized study. 8 In another retrospective study, longer fasting time was associated with higher incidence of vasovagal reaction. 9 However, coronary intervention differs from those procedures. In the setting of coronary procedures, retrospective studies 7,10,11 found no differences regarding adverse outcomes between fasting and nonfasting patients. The randomized CHOW NOW (Can we Safely Have Our Patients Eat With Cardiac Catheterization - Nix Or alloW) trial was designed to address that question but has not been published to date. More recently, a small, randomized trial showed that a ' heart-healthy diet ' before a coronary procedure improved patient satisfaction. 12 However, the lack of a well-designed published randomized study regarding coronary procedures safety is still hindering changes in daily practice. 2 Besides improving patients ' comfort and satisfaction, such changes in practice would also prevent procedures cancelation caused by nonfasting patients, and thus improve catheterization laboratories ef fi ciency.

On-site cardiac surgery allowed complex and high-risk procedures to be performed, which were also included. Patients presenting hemodynamic instability, coronary emergency, pregnancy or breastfeeding, those protected by law (under guardianship or curatorship), those with artifi cial nutrition or requiring fasting for a medical reason and those undergoing a noncoronary procedure at the same time (for example percutaneous aortic valvular replacement or right-heart catheterization) were excluded. Also, patients couldn ' t be included twice in the trial.

texts.orig: PROCEDURE. The coronary procedure (angiography and/or PCI) was performed in both groups as usual, according to routine practice and current guidelines. Local anesthesia using subcutaneous lidocaine 1% (1 to 20 mL) was administered around the arterial access site. After sheath introduction, intra-arterial vasodilators (2.5-mg verapamil and 1-mg isosorbide dinitrate) and unfractionated heparin (3,000 IU) were administered (radial access only). Additional heparin (total of 50-100 IU/kg intravenous [IV]) was administered if PCI or fractional fl ow reserve measurements were performed. The contrast agent used was iodixanol (Visipaque 320, GE Healthcare), an iso-osmolar contrast agent.

texts.orig: STATISTICS AND OUTCOMES. As this trial aimed to determine whether allowing food and liquid intake before elective or semiurgent coronary angiography was noninferior to fasting in terms of safety and well-being of patients, the primary endpoint was a composite of vasovagal reaction, hypoglycemia (de fi ned by blood sugar # 0.7 g/L), and isolated nausea and/or vomiting occurring up to the end of the 4 hours postprocedure monitoring. Vasovagal reaction was de fi ned by 2 of the 3 following criteria, in absence of another cause: 1) nausea, vomiting, paleness, or sweating; 2) low systolic blood pressure < 100 mm Hg (or drop of > 15% if already lower than 100 mm Hg); 3) low heart rate < 60 beats/min (or drop > 15% if already lower than 60 beats/min).

texts.orig: Based on the literature data, assuming a percentage of the primary outcome (vasovagal reaction, hypoglycemia, or isolated nausea and/or vomiting) of 5% in the fasting and nonfasting groups, the analysis of 736 patients would yield 80% power, with a 1-tailed alpha risk of 5%, to show the noninferiority of the nonfasting strategy to the usual fasting strategy before the procedure, with regard to the occurrence of the primary outcome, considering a noninferiority margin of 4%. A margin of 4% was considered based on expert consensus within our steering committee, who deemed it acceptable considering the primary outcome, which did not encompass mortality or other serious adverse events. Thus, noninferiority was de fi ned as the upper bound of the 1-tailed 95% CI of the absolute between-group difference in the percentage of patients reaching the primary outcome lying below the threshold of 4%.

texts.text: DISCUSSION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The TONIC trial assessed the impact of a nonfasting strategy compared with the usual fasting strategy regarding safety and well-being for patients undergoing elective or semiurgent coronary procedures. We demonstrated, in both modi fi ed intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations, that a nonfasting strategy was noninferior to the usual fasting strategy before coronary procedures with regard to the occurrence of a composite primary outcome comprising vasovagal reaction, hypoglycemia, and isolated nausea and/or vomiting, and of the occurrence of each of the individual components of the primary composite outcome. Regarding safety, no adverse events related to food and liquid intake occurred, and no differences were observed regarding aspiration pneumonia and contrast-induced acute kidney injuries. Overall, patients were satis fi ed in both groups, and the majority of them would prefer free access to food and drinks if they had to undergo another procedure in the future.

texts.orig: OVERALL SAFETY. Procedure safety has always been 1 of the main concerns of the operators. Highosmolality contrast agents used in the past induced nausea and vomiting in almost 25% of patients. 13 Moreover, complications requiring general anesthesia and intubation were more likely to occur at the initial development of interventional cardiology. For this reason and despite little evidence supporting it, fasting has always been recommended to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration in such scenario. Nowadays, those risks are very low for nonemergency procedures. 3,4,5,7 Moreover, newer nonionic contrast agents induce mild nausea in only 3% of patients. 13 Our results con fi rm the very low incidence of pulmonary aspiration (n ¼ 2, 0.3%) and of nausea/ vomiting (n ¼ 12, 1.6%) but also of major adverse events requiring intubation: only 1 (0.3%) patient suffered a coronary perforation complicated by tamponade and cardiac arrest. This very low frequency of adverse events is likely to be the main reason for the absence of difference between nonfasting and fasting strategies observed in previously published retrospective and nonrandomized studies. 7,10,11

texts.orig: FASTING SAFETY. In the fi eld of interventional electrophysiology, the study of Bode et al 14 randomized 201 patients planned for cardiac implantable electronic device procedures under local anesthesia and moderate sedation to a fasting vs nonfasting strategy. The results reported better patients ' wellbeing with no adverse safety outcomes in the nonfasting group. In the fi eld of coronary interventions, the results of the CHOW NOW trial presented as an abstract were promising but never published in a peer-reviewed journal, preventing any practice change, as stated in the SCAI 2021 guidelines. 2 More recently, a smaller randomized trial compared a ' heart-healthy ' diet (speci fi ed diet low in fats and acidity) vs fasting and demonstrated improved patient satisfaction in the nonfasting group, 12 but was underpowered to address safety. Moreover, patients in the nonfasting group were assigned to a speci fi c diet, which could be too restrictive to implement in daily practice.

texts.orig: PATIENTS ' WELL-BEING. As expected, nonfasting patients were signi fi cantly less hungry and less thirsty than fasting patients. For future procedures, most patients (79%) would prefer free access to food and drinks over fasting, with higher values (87% vs 71%; P < 0.0001) in the nonfasting group, probably because they just experienced improved comfort without added risks. However, fasting did not in fl uence global patient satisfaction and perceived pain of the procedure, as reported in previous studies. 14,16 This reinforces the idea that what probably matters is not the food intake in itself but patients ' beliefs and perception of the waiting time and the procedure. If a patient is convinced fasting is better, forcing him to eat would probably be detrimental to his well-being and likely to induce a nocebo effect. Thus, patients should be informed that eating is safe, and then be free to decide.

If a patient is convinced fasting is better, forcing him to eat would probably be detrimental to his well-being and likely to induce a nocebo effect. Thus, patients should be informed that eating is safe, and then be free to decide.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: STUDY LIMITATIONS. First, this was a monocentric study and results may need to be con fi rmed in larger multicentric randomized studies with variety of local practices. Second, among the 41 biological hypoglycemia cases observed, only 4 (10%) were associated with symptoms and required speci fi c glucose treatment. However, whether we consider hypoglycemia or symptomatic hypoglycemia, noninferiority of the nonfasting intervention was present. Third, a very low (but still present, 4%) number of patients in the fasting group did not comply with the instructions and ate food. Although these crossovers may have changed the results of the study, a per-protocol analysis was planned and found similar results. Also, fasting times were longer than expected in both groups, with mean fasting times of 3 hours vs 15 hours in the nonfasting and in the fasting groups, respectively. Even in the nonfasting group, few patients had food or liquid intake very close to the procedure. It is, however, dif fi cult to give a precise intra-day schedule for procedures, and patients sometimes wait longer than expected. We did not ask patients for their perception of the waiting time, which might have felt longer in the fasting group. Last, a minor limitation of our study was missing data for some of the secondary outcomes: 19 satisfaction questionnaires (3%) were not retrieved, 246 blood tests (33%) at day 3 were not performed, and 71 patients (10%) were lost during follow-up at day 7. Nonetheless, there was no missing data for the primary outcome.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The TONIC trial demonstrates noninferiority in regard to safety of a nonfasting strategy to the routine fasting strategy for all patients undergoing elective or semi-urgent coronary procedures, with no foodrelated adverse event. A nonfasting strategy could improve patients ' comfort as well as catheterization laboratories ef fi ciency.
